# Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression {#b10} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Lecture 10, you can - rewrite benchmark and comparison questions as tests of a zero contrast; - complete and communicate a two-sided test using the seven-step workflow; - distinguish a p-value, a significance level, and a test decision; - describe Type I error, Type II error, and power in context; - explain when a one-sided alternative is legitimate and why this course's exams are two-sided; - separate statistical significance from magnitude, practical importance, and causality; - interpret the zero-null test printed for a regression coefficient. ::: ::: {.driving-question} Driving question

Launch the product or wait. Approve the loan or decline. Decisions made from data can err in two directions, and the two mistakes usually cost very different amounts.

Every test can be wrong in two ways. Which wrong call is which, what makes wrong calls rarer, and how does all of this reappear in a regression table? ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Total preparation time: about 25 minutes.
Video preparation (15 minutes)
Review Introduction to Hypothesis Testing and watch Examples Identifying Type I and Type II Errors. Focus on two-sided tests, decision errors, and why "do not reject" is not "accept." All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.
**Reactivate (8 minutes).** Suppose R reports the following coefficient row: | Estimate | SE | t | p-value | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | -0.290 | 0.058 | -5.00 | < 0.001 | State the hypotheses being tested and give a careful one-sentence statistical conclusion. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation The default two-sided coefficient test is $H_0:\beta=0$ against $H_1:\beta\ne0$. Because the p-value is below 0.05, reject $H_0$: the data provide evidence that the population-model coefficient differs from zero. A full interpretation still needs the outcome, predictor, units, held-fixed variables, population, and causal limit. ::: **Predict (2 minutes).** Answer the one-click Mentimeter question posted on Canvas before you come to class: a test at $\alpha=0.05$ returns $p=0.20$. Has the study **shown that the null is true** --- yes, no, or cannot tell? Commit to an answer; the lecture resolves it. Review [Mathematics Refresher: zero contrasts, inequalities, and standardisation](../resources/math-refresher.html) if needed. ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In class The session opens with the usual four-minute entry quiz on the prep videos, then turns to the driving question. Lecture 9 delivered one complete test. This final lecture makes testing a *routine*: one recipe, an honest account of the two ways any decision can be wrong, and the payoff --- the same machinery reappearing, unchanged, in every regression table you will read from Intermediate onwards.

Video explanations (review): Introduction to Hypothesis Testing and Type I and Type II Errors.

### Why zero is the universal benchmark Many empirical questions ask whether a population contrast is absent: - difference from a target: $\delta=\mu-15$; - difference in probabilities: $\delta_p=p-0.50$; - difference between two group means: $\mu_1-\mu_0$; - a regression slope: $\beta_j$. In every case, "no difference" or "no linear association" becomes $$ H_0:\theta=0 \qquad\text{versus}\qquad H_1:\theta\ne0. $$ Testing a non-zero benchmark can always be rewritten as a test of a zero-valued contrast --- Lecture 9's gap device. This common structure is the bridge from Basic inference to regression inference: learn to test one zero, and you can test them all. ### The seven-step testing workflow Use the same sequence every time --- on the exam, in your EiA venture, in any report you ever write: 1. Define the population parameter and its units. 2. State $H_0$ and the two-sided $H_1$ **before** inspecting the result. 3. Check the sampling and model conditions. 4. Calculate the estimate and its SE under the null model. 5. Standardise: $(\text{estimate}-0)/\text{SE}$. 6. Calculate the two-sided p-value and compare it with the pre-specified significance level $\alpha$. 7. Report the estimate, uncertainty, decision, contextual meaning, and limits. The significance level $\alpha$ is a long-run decision threshold, commonly 0.05, fixed in advance. The p-value is calculated from the observed data under $H_0$. They are not the same object: one is a rule, the other a result. If $p\le\alpha$, reject $H_0$. If $p>\alpha$, **do not reject** $H_0$ --- and do not say "accept $H_0$." This resolves the prep prediction: a study with $p=0.20$ has *not* shown the null is true; it may simply lack the precision to distinguish a meaningful non-zero parameter from zero. The power section below makes that precise. ::: {#exm-b10-launch-test} ## Worked example: a proportion test by hand An accelerator claims that half of its alumni launch a trading venture within a year. In a random sample of 400 former participants, 232 had launched. Let $p$ be the launch proportion in the alumni frame and define $\delta_p=p-0.50$. Test $H_0:\delta_p=0$ against $H_1:\delta_p\ne0$ at 5%, voicing every arithmetic step. - **Estimate.** $\hat p=232/400=0.58$, so the estimated gap is $\widehat\delta_p=0.58-0.50=0.08$, eight percentage points. - **Conditions under the null.** $np_0=400(0.50)=200$ and $n(1-p_0)=200$, both far above 10 --- the normal approximation is safe. - **Null SE.** Under $H_0$ the true proportion is 0.50, so $\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/400}=\sqrt{0.25/400} =\sqrt{0.000625}=0.025$. - **Standardise.** $z=0.08/0.025=3.20$: the observed gap sits 3.2 null standard errors above zero. - **p-value and decision.** The two-sided p-value is $2\,P(Z\le-3.20)\approx 0.0014 < 0.05$: reject $H_0$. The sample provides strong evidence that the frame launch proportion differs from 50%; the positive estimate places it above. Note step 4's subtlety: the SE was computed with $p_0=0.50$, not with $\hat p$ --- the test measures how surprising the sample is *in the null's world*, so the null supplies the spread. ::: ### The Shark Tank deal proportion, in R The same recipe on our reproducible sample of 100: is the frame's deal proportion different from 50%? Every object is constructed on screen: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) set.seed(123) sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE) pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ] n <- nrow(pitch_sample) phat <- mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show) # sample deal proportion p0 <- 0.50 # null value deal_gap <- phat - p0 # estimated gap c(n = n, phat = phat, p0 = p0, deal_gap = deal_gap) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n phat p0 deal_gap 100.00 0.64 0.50 0.14 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} null_se <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n) z_value <- deal_gap / null_se two_sided_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_value)) c( null_standard_error = null_se, z_statistic = z_value, two_sided_p_value = two_sided_p ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` null_standard_error z_statistic two_sided_p_value 0.050000000 2.800000000 0.005110261 ``` ::: ::: The estimate is $\widehat\delta_p=0.14$, fourteen percentage points. The null SE is $\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/100}=0.05$, the statistic is $z=2.80$, and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. The success--failure condition holds under the null: $np_0=50$ and $n(1-p_0)=50$. Reject the zero-gap null at 5%: the random sample provides evidence that the recorded-pitch-frame deal proportion differs from 50%, and the positive estimate places it above. ### Interval and test: report both Step 7 of the workflow says a decision alone is not a report. A large-sample 95% interval for the proportion uses the estimated SE: $$ \hat p\pm1.96 \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}. $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimated_se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n) proportion_ci <- phat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * estimated_se gap_ci <- proportion_ci - p0 c(proportion_lower = proportion_ci[1], proportion_upper = proportion_ci[2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` proportion_lower proportion_upper 0.54592 0.73408 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(gap_lower = gap_ci[1], gap_upper = gap_ci[2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gap_lower gap_upper 0.04592 0.23408 ``` ::: ::: The proportion interval is approximately $(0.546,\,0.734)$; the equivalent gap interval is $(0.046,\,0.234)$, which excludes zero and agrees with the test decision here. ::: {.optional-box} Optional: estimated versus null standard errors
Look closely: the test divided by the **null** SE $\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}=0.050$, while the interval used the **estimated** SE $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}=0.048$. The test asks how surprising the sample is if $H_0$ were true, so the null supplies the spread; the interval makes no null assumption, so the data supply it. Because these are not exactly the same procedure, interval and test decisions need not match perfectly when a result sits very near the boundary. Exact equivalence requires an interval obtained by inverting the same test --- beyond this course. For the mean-gap t procedures of Lecture 9 the same SE is used in both, so there the match is exact. ::: ### What a p-value is not The two-sided p-value is $$ P\!\left(|\text{test statistic}| \ge|\text{observed statistic}|\mid H_0\right) $$ --- and nothing else. Before the break you receive four sentences about the launch test of @exm-b10-launch-test ($z=3.20$, $p\approx 0.0014$). Each one is wrong. In pairs, correct all four; the plenary compares repairs. ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Try it: correct the four wrong p-value sentences *Sentence 1 (you).* "There is only a 0.14% probability that the launch proportion really is 50%." *Sentence 2 (you).* "The result has a 0.14% probability of being due to chance." *Sentence 3 (you).* "Such a tiny p-value shows that the launch proportion is far above 50%." *Sentence 4 (you).* "The tiny p-value proves that the accelerator causes its alumni to launch ventures." ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. A p-value is not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$. Correct: "If the launch proportion were exactly 50%, a sample gap at least this far from zero in either direction would occur in about 0.14% of random samples." 2. The p-value is computed *assuming* chance alone (the null model) generated the gap; it is the probability of data this extreme under that assumption, not the probability that the assumption holds. 3. A p-value measures surprise, not size. The magnitude is the estimate: 8 percentage points, with an interval around it. A tiny p-value can accompany a tiny gap when $n$ is huge. 4. Significance says nothing about why. Alumni self-selected into the accelerator; without a design that isolates its effect, "causes" is unsupported. Correct: the frame's launch proportion differs from 50%. ::: ::: ### Type I error, Type II error, and power A test is a decision rule, and any decision rule can be wrong in exactly two ways: | Reality | Reject $H_0$ | Do not reject $H_0$ | |---|---|---| | $H_0$ true | Type I error | Correct decision | | $H_1$ true | Correct decision | Type II error | The significance level controls the first: $$ P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true})=\alpha. $$ **Power** is the ability to avoid the second: $$ \text{power}=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_1\text{ true}). $$ For the launch test, in context: a **Type I error** would be concluding that the alumni launch proportion differs from 50% when it is exactly 50% --- crying wolf about a fictitious difference, embarrassing the analyst who advises repricing the programme. A **Type II error** would be failing to detect a launch proportion that genuinely differs from 50% --- missing a real signal because the sample was too small or noisy. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) z_grid <- seq(-4.5, 6.5, length.out = 1600) critical <- qnorm(0.975) panel_levels <- c("Null is true", "An alternative value is true") test_curves <- rbind( data.frame(z = z_grid, density = dnorm(z_grid, mean = 0), panel = panel_levels[1]), data.frame(z = z_grid, density = dnorm(z_grid, mean = 2.5), panel = panel_levels[2]) ) test_curves$panel <- factor(test_curves$panel, levels = panel_levels) rejection <- subset(test_curves, z <= -critical | z >= critical) rejection$side <- ifelse(rejection$z < 0, "left", "right") panel_labels <- data.frame( z = c(0, 3.6), density = c(0.13, 0.14), label = c("do not reject", "power"), panel = factor(panel_levels[c(1, 2)], levels = panel_levels) ) alpha_labels <- data.frame( z = c(-2.5, 2.5), density = c(0.028, 0.028), label = c("alpha/2", "alpha/2"), panel = factor(panel_levels[c(1, 1)], levels = panel_levels) ) ggplot(test_curves, aes(z, density)) + geom_area(data = rejection, aes(group = side, fill = panel), alpha = 0.4) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-critical, critical), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) + geom_line(aes(colour = panel), linewidth = 0.9) + geom_text(data = panel_labels, aes(label = label), colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) + geom_text(data = alpha_labels, aes(label = label), parse = TRUE, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.1) + facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "fixed") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Null is true" = "#D55E00", "An alternative value is true" = "#009E73"), guide = "none") + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Null is true" = "#17324D", "An alternative value is true" = "#0072B2"), guide = "none") + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 6)) + labs(x = "z statistic", y = "Density") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"), strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Two-sided testing at α = 0.05. Left: when the null is true, the z statistic follows the dark curve and the orange rejection regions have total probability 0.05 — the Type I error rate. Right: when a positive alternative is true, the statistic follows the shifted blue curve; the green area is the power, and the unshaded middle is the Type II error probability. Both panels use the same axes.](b10-testing-errors-power_files/figure-html/fig-b10-errors-power-1.png){#fig-b10-errors-power width=672} ::: ::: In both panels of @fig-b10-errors-power, the horizontal axis is the possible z statistic, the vertical axis is density, and probability is area. The dashed vertical lines mark the same two-sided critical values, $\pm 1.96$. In the left panel the null is true: the two orange rejection tails have total probability $\alpha=0.05$, which is exactly the Type I error rate --- the test is *built* to cry wolf 5% of the time. In the right panel a particular positive alternative is true, so the curve has shifted: the green area is the power, and whatever probability remains between the dashed lines is the Type II error rate. Four levers raise power: - a larger true distance from zero (an effect that is easier to see); - a larger sample (a smaller SE); - lower unexplained variation (also a smaller SE); - a larger $\alpha$ --- but this lever is a trade-off, not a free gain: widening the rejection region catches more true effects *and* raises the Type I error rate in lockstep. ### One-sided alternatives A two-sided test asks whether a parameter differs from zero in **either** direction. A one-sided test asks a directional question chosen before the sample is examined: | Research question | Alternative | Relevant tail(s) | |---|---|---| | Does the gap differ from zero? | $H_1:\delta\ne0$ | both tails | | Is the gap below zero? | $H_1:\delta<0$ | left tail | | Is the gap above zero? | $H_1:\delta>0$ | right tail | In all three cases the test statistic is compared with its distribution under the zero boundary $H_0:\delta=0$. What changes is which values count as evidence for the stated alternative --- that is, where the rejection region sits. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) alpha_tail <- 0.05 tail_df <- 99 tail_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1400) critical_two <- qt(c(alpha_tail / 2, 1 - alpha_tail / 2), df = tail_df) critical_left <- qt(alpha_tail, df = tail_df) critical_right <- qt(1 - alpha_tail, df = tail_df) panel_levels <- c("Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided") null_curve <- do.call(rbind, lapply(panel_levels, function(p) { data.frame(x = tail_grid, density = dt(tail_grid, df = tail_df), panel = p) })) null_curve$panel <- factor(null_curve$panel, levels = panel_levels) rejection <- rbind( cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Two-sided" & x <= critical_two[1]), side = "left"), cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Two-sided" & x >= critical_two[2]), side = "right"), cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Left-sided" & x <= critical_left), side = "left"), cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Right-sided" & x >= critical_right), side = "right") ) critical_lines <- data.frame( x = c(critical_two, critical_left, critical_right), panel = factor(c("Two-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided"), levels = panel_levels) ) panel_labels <- data.frame( x = c(-2.8, 2.8, -2.8, 2.8, 0, 0, 0), density = c(0.035, 0.035, 0.035, 0.035, 0.42, 0.42, 0.42), label = c("2.5%", "2.5%", "5%", "5%", "H[1] : delta != 0", "H[1] : delta < 0", "H[1] : delta > 0"), parse_me = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE), panel = factor(c("Two-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided"), levels = panel_levels) ) ggplot(null_curve, aes(x, density)) + geom_area(data = rejection, aes(group = side), fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.6) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_vline(data = critical_lines, aes(xintercept = x), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) + geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_text(data = subset(panel_labels, !parse_me), aes(label = label), colour = "#17324D", size = 2.9) + geom_text(data = subset(panel_labels, parse_me), aes(label = label), parse = TRUE, colour = "#5B6976", size = 3.1) + facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = "fixed") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-3, 0, 3)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4), limits = c(0, 0.44), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) + labs(x = "t statistic", y = "Density") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"), strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Rejection regions at α = 0.05 for the two-sided and both one-sided alternatives, on the same null t distribution (df = 99). The two-sided test places 2.5% in each tail; a one-sided test moves the full 5% into the tail named by its alternative, so its critical value is closer to zero in that direction.](b10-testing-errors-power_files/figure-html/fig-b10-one-sided-1.png){#fig-b10-one-sided width=672} ::: ::: Compare @fig-b10-one-sided with the left panel of @fig-b10-errors-power: same logic, different placement of the 5%. Moving the full 5% into one tail pulls that critical value closer to zero, so a one-sided test is *more* able to detect an effect in its chosen direction --- a power gain. The price: results in the opposite direction, however extreme, do not support the stated alternative at all. That power gain is exactly why the direction must follow from the research question and be **fixed before the data are inspected**. Choosing the tail because the observed estimate happens to point that way --- or simply to obtain a smaller p-value --- silently doubles the true Type I error rate: you would take the 5% tail on whichever side the noise landed. For Lecture 9's equity-gap statistic, $t=-2.91$ with $df=99$: - the two-sided p-value is about 0.0045; - a **pre-specified** left-sided alternative $H_1:\delta<0$ gives about 0.0023; - a **pre-specified** right-sided alternative $H_1:\delta>0$ gives about 0.9977. The negative estimate agrees with the left-sided alternative and points away from the right-sided one. Course convention, on the exam and in every chapter: **tests are two-sided**, because in business research a difference in either direction is usually relevant --- and because the convention removes any temptation to pick the convenient tail. ### Preview: the test attached to a regression slope R applies the same zero-null logic to every regression coefficient. Consider the simple model of initial equity offered on season, fitted to all 1,441 records: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} preview_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks) summary(preview_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 20.4565874 0.46442667 44.04697 4.922706e-269 season -0.8241241 0.04752298 -17.34159 2.514546e-61 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(preview_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 19.5455616 21.3676132 season -0.9173458 -0.7309023 ``` ::: ::: Read the `season` row with the vocabulary you now own. The **estimate** is $-0.824$: about 0.82 percentage points less equity offered per additional season. The **SE**, 0.048, is its sampling uncertainty in the same units. The **t value**, $-17.3$, is estimate divided by SE --- step 5 of the workflow. The **p-value** belongs to the printed two-sided test $$ H_0:\beta_1=0 \qquad\text{versus}\qquad H_1:\beta_1\ne0, $$ and the 95% **interval** $(-0.92,\,-0.73)$ excludes zero, agreeing with the rejection. Every column is a Lecture 9--10 object wearing a regression name. What the row does *not* say: this is an observational time association, not a causal effect of moving a pitch to a later season. Intermediate begins from this familiar estimate--SE--t--p-value structure and adds careful coefficient interpretation, multiple predictors, and model diagnostics. ::: {.caveat-box} What a significant result does and does not establish Three separations to carry out of this course. **Significance is not magnitude:** a tiny effect can be significant in a large sample, and a meaningful effect can be non-significant in a small or noisy one --- the p-value measures surprise under the null, the estimate measures size. **Significance is not causation:** none of this lecture's machinery knows whether the predictor was randomly assigned. **And no test repairs the frame:** selection into the recorded-pitch file, measurement of "deal" as an on-air agreement, and dependence between observations are untouched by any p-value. The standing reporting list, for every analysis from now on: the estimate in substantive units; a confidence interval; the p-value or decision; whether the magnitude matters for the business question; and the sampling, measurement, and causal limits. ::: ### Answering the driving question The two wrong calls: rejecting a true null (Type I, rate set by $\alpha$) and missing a true effect (Type II, rate cut by power). Wrong calls become rarer with more data, less noise, bigger true effects --- and, for Type I only, a stricter $\alpha$, at the price of more Type II. And the regression table? Each coefficient row *is* a Lecture 9 test: estimate, SE, t, two-sided p against zero, interval. That closes the arc of QM Basic. Ten lectures ago a Shark Tank pitch was an anecdote. Now you can define events and variables on a frame, describe their distributions, condition without confusing directions, model sampling variation, and turn "our sample mean is 12.76" into a defensible, properly hedged claim about a population --- with its uncertainty, its decision, and its limits stated. That is the difference between an opinion with a spreadsheet and evidence. **Next:** Tutorial 4 rehearses Lectures 9--10 in exam format, and the Mock Exam then integrates the whole course under exam conditions. The story itself continues next year: QM Intermediate picks up exactly where today's regression preview left off, and the coefficient row you can already read becomes the central object of six lectures on linear regression. ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class Total practice time: about 65 minutes. ### Retrieval (10 minutes) 1. Why can most comparison hypotheses be written as a parameter equal to zero? 2. What is the difference between $\alpha$ and a p-value? 3. What is a Type I error? 4. What is a Type II error? 5. Name three factors that increase power. 6. Why is "do not reject" different from "accept"? 7. What does $H_0:\beta_j=0$ mean in a regression model? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. Subtracting the benchmark or reference value creates a contrast; "no difference" corresponds to a zero contrast. 2. $\alpha$ is a pre-specified long-run decision threshold; the p-value is calculated from the observed statistic under the null. 3. Rejecting $H_0$ when it is true. 4. Not rejecting $H_0$ when a specified alternative is true. 5. Any three of: larger sample size, larger true effect, lower noise, or larger $\alpha$ (the last at the cost of more Type I errors). 6. A non-significant result may simply be too imprecise to distinguish a meaningful parameter from zero. 7. Holding the other included predictors fixed, the population-model coefficient for predictor $j$ is zero. ::: ### From worked to faded, then unassisted (20 minutes) Re-read the hand-worked launch test (@exm-b10-launch-test). Then complete the same recipe with new numbers: in 200 independent trials there are 120 successes, and the benchmark is $p_0=0.50$. *Step 1 (given).* $\hat p=120/200=0.60$, so $\widehat\delta_p=0.10$; the null counts are $200(0.50)=100$ successes and 100 failures, both above 10. *Step 2 (you).* Calculate the null SE and the z statistic. *Step 3 (you).* The two-sided p-value and the 5% decision, in context. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer $\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/200}\approx 0.0354$, so $z=0.10/0.0354\approx 2.83$ and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. Reject the zero-gap null at 5%: the data provide evidence that the success proportion differs from 50%, with the positive estimate placing it above. ::: Now unassisted: 1. A sample of $n=49$ difference scores has $\bar d=3$ and $s_d=14$. Test $H_0:\delta=0$ against $H_1:\delta\ne0$ at 5%. 2. Describe the Type I and Type II errors for the 120-of-200 test above, in context. 3. A multiple-regression coefficient is $-0.290$ percentage points per €100,000, with SE 0.058 and a large $df$. Calculate its t statistic and approximate 95% interval, and interpret the row. 4. A coefficient estimate is economically negligible but has $p<0.001$. Explain how both facts can be true. 5. State two reasons the regression preview cannot support a causal conclusion. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. The SE is $14/\sqrt{49}=2$, so $t=3/2=1.50$ with $df=48$; the two-sided p-value is about 0.14. Do not reject the zero mean-difference null at 5% --- which is not evidence that the difference is zero. 2. Type I: concluding the population success proportion differs from 0.50 when it equals 0.50. Type II: failing to detect a genuine specified difference from 0.50. 3. $t=-0.290/0.058=-5.00$. With a large $df$, the 95% interval is approximately $-0.290\pm1.96(0.058)=(-0.404,\,-0.176)$ percentage points per €100,000. Holding the model's other predictors fixed, an additional €100,000 requested is associated with between about 0.18 and 0.40 percentage points less fitted equity; reject the zero-coefficient null. 4. A very large sample or low noise makes the SE tiny, so even a negligible coefficient sits many SEs from zero. Precision does not confer importance. 5. Season was not randomly assigned, and omitted factors, selection, reverse direction, or measurement error can all remain. ::: ### One-sided reasoning (10 minutes) Lecture 9's equity-gap test gave $t=-2.91$ with $df=99$. 1. State all three p-values: two-sided, left-sided ($H_1:\delta<0$), and right-sided ($H_1:\delta>0$). 2. Which of the three alternatives would have been legitimate to pre-specify, and what determines that? 3. A classmate, seeing the negative estimate, switches to the left-sided alternative "because it fits the data." What exactly is wrong? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. Two-sided: about 0.0045. Left-sided: about 0.0023 (the single left tail beyond $-2.91$). Right-sided: about 0.9977 (everything to the right of $-2.91$). 2. Any of the three --- **provided** it was fixed before inspecting the sample and follows from the research question. Legitimacy is about timing and motivation, not about which alternative is "correct." 3. Choosing the tail after seeing the estimate means the 5% rejection mass would follow the data to whichever side the noise landed, so the true Type I error rate is doubled to about 10%. The smaller p-value is bought by an invalid procedure. Course convention: two-sided, always, on the exam. ::: ### Spaced review: one item each from Lectures 9 and 5 (10 minutes) 1. *(Lecture 9.)* A 95% confidence interval for a mean gap is $(0.4,\,5.2)$ units. State the 5% two-sided test decision without computing, and name one thing the interval reports that the decision does not. 2. *(Lecture 5.)* In the full file, the correlation between season and initial equity offered is about $-0.42$. Interpret this number in one sentence, and state one claim it cannot support. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. The interval excludes zero, so the matched two-sided test rejects $H_0:\delta=0$ at 5%. The interval additionally shows direction, plausible magnitude (0.4 to 5.2 units), and precision. 2. Season and offered equity have a moderate negative linear association: later-season pitches tend to offer less equity. It cannot support a causal claim --- nothing assigned pitches to seasons, and other factors changed over time. ::: ### Worked exam interpretation (10 minutes) **Question (Mock Exam Q5 pattern).** In a simple random sample of 400 former accelerator participants, 232 had launched a trading venture within one year; a two-sided test of $H_0:p=0.50$ is planned. The same study fits a regression of monthly revenue (thousands of euros) on weekly mentoring hours; one row of the output is: ```text Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) 95% CI mentoring_hours 0.80 0.25 3.20 0.0016 [0.31, 1.29] ``` Complete the proportion test at 5% (a large-sample 95% interval for $p$ is $(0.532,\,0.628)$), define a Type I error for it, name two power levers that hold $\alpha$ fixed, and interpret the regression row without causal language. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer Under $H_0$, $np_0=n(1-p_0)=200\ge 10$. $\hat p=232/400=0.58$, $\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/400}=0.025$, and $z=0.08/0.025=3.20$ with two-sided p-value about 0.0014: reject $H_0$; the frame launch proportion differs from 50%, plausibly between 53.2% and 62.8% --- the interval excludes 0.50, agreeing with the test. A Type I error would be concluding the launch proportion differs from 50% when it equals 50%. With $\alpha$ fixed, power rises with a larger sample or lower outcome variability (or a larger true gap, though that is not chosen). The regression row: each additional weekly mentoring hour is associated with 0.80 thousand euros more fitted monthly revenue; $t=0.80/0.25=3.20$, $p=0.0016$, and the interval $(0.31,\,1.29)$ excludes zero, so reject $H_0:\beta=0$. Mentoring hours were not randomly assigned, so this is an association, not a causal effect. ::: ### Make it yours (5 minutes) :::: {.utility-prompt} Utility: two sentences Think of your EiA venture --- or any business you know well. Name one yes-or-no claim you will realistically have to defend with data (our conversion rate beats the sector's 3%; our average order exceeds the break-even basket), and write two sentences: first state it as a two-sided zero-contrast test and say which of the two errors would be more costly for you and why, then name the one power lever you could actually pull before your next pitch. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture.
